summary:
Nothing in Honduran law criminalises being trans. The Penal Code, as amended by Decree No. 23-2013 and in force since March 2017, treats hatred or contempt based on sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating circumstance in criminal responsibility (Article 27); punishes anyone who arbitrarily blocks, restricts or denies individual or collective rights, or refuses a professional service, on those grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages (Article 321); and punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a person or group on listed grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity with three to five years' imprisonment and fines of L.50,000 to L.300,000 (Article 321-A). A name change for LGBTI persons is approved in Honduras.

The violence picture is severe. Honduras is among the most dangerous countries in the Americas for trans women. Human Rights Watch's May 2009 report Not Worth a Penny documents police rape, assault and extortion of transgender people in Honduras alongside the domestic laws then in force. The US State Department's 2021 Human Rights Report for Honduras lists violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons among the country's significant human-rights issues, together with extrajudicial killings, torture, and lack of accountability for gender-based violence.

Vicky Hernández v. Honduras, heard by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case worldwide. The Court's 2021 judgment held the Honduran state responsible for the 2009 killing of trans activist Vicky Hernández and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime, and ordered reforms including legal gender recognition; Honduras has partially implemented them. Human Rights Watch finds that states in the region exclude transgender women from their femicide legal frameworks, with Guatemalan officials describing them as "not biological women", a framing that shapes how such killings are classified and pursued.

Impunity is the practical risk behind the statutes. The LAWG Education Fund report Left in the Dark finds that Honduras and El Salvador record some of the world's highest rates of violence against women and LGBTI persons, and that LGBTI people, trans women especially, face major obstacles to justice. The report attributes impunity to under-reporting, absent police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources, and intentional mishandling of cases, concluding that the institutions "fail to effectively investigate and prosecute".

Police powers over public space are a live constraint. The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs permits police to raid city streets and arrest anyone who "goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals"; LGBTQ organisations document repeated use of that provision as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space. Detention carries a further hazard: trans women in Honduras' national penitentiaries are held in the men's system, and Human Rights Watch reports in 2020 that this placement can lead to physical and sexual abuse.

Partner recognition is closed. The 2005 constitutional amendment expressly bans same-sex marriage and de facto unions, refuses to recognise same-sex marriages or unions performed legally in other countries (Article 112), and prohibits same-sex couples from adopting (Article 116). Same-sex couples and same-sex-headed households receive none of the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples.
tangentialFactors:
Trans visibility and the security cost attached to it run in parallel in Honduras. A trans activist and co-founder of Asociación Cozumel Trans ran for Congress in Francisco Morazán for the PINU party at the 26 November 2017 election, potentially becoming the first openly trans officeholder; the same period produced Kendra Stefani Jordany's 2017 primary win and Claudia Spellman's 2012 run for LIBRE. Victoria Gomez sought asylum in Spain after threats and attacks in Tegucigalpa, an example of the price political visibility carried.

Official hostility is stated rather than merely structural. President Juan Orlando Hernández said on 12 October 2018 that personally, as a Christian, he is against same-sex marriage, and the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association has urged President Xiomara Castro to stop "immoral laws"; the same figure described the approved name change for LGBTI persons as an "aberration in God's eyes". The two major parties have largely ignored LGBTQ rights, only a handful of dissident members of the Democratic Unification Party engaged with the LGBT community, and three candidates who backed same-sex marriage before the November 2017 elections all failed to win National Congress seats.

The regional pattern is documented rather than assumed. Central American states exclude transgender women from femicide legal frameworks, and Honduras and El Salvador sit together at the top of regional violence rankings; a Reuters feature on Central American LGBT people fleeing for their lives frames the same flight dynamic. A dated archive of Honduran LGBT news from 2004 to 2011 corroborates the violence timeline, recording an August 2004 church protest against state recognition of three gay groups, 2009-10 reporting on an LGBT activist murdered amid violence and impunity, and post-coup abuses against the gay community.

Public organising continues despite this. About 400 people marched in a pride parade in San Pedro Sula in July 2017. Under the Constitution, citizens may establish and associate with political parties and interest groups, though early attempts to register an LGBTQ rights group in the 1980s met government opposition and extended delays, and the first organisations arose in response to the HIV/AIDS pandemic without legal standing. In 2004 the government extended formal recognition to three LGBTQ interest groups despite organised protests from the Catholic Church, Pentecostals and conservative legislators.
localsOnly:
Placement in custody operates on birth sex. Trans women are held within the men's national prison system, with no placement-by-gender-identity policy in force. At Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara, LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the "La Isla" module beside the mentally-ill unit; trans women are forced to cut their hair, barred from presenting as women — officers state that "ellas son hombres" — and denied conjugal visits. At Penitenciaria de Marcala, authorities seized one trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after intervention by the torture-prevention centre CPTRT was she isolated from the men and her belongings returned. Placement is documented as birth-sex based, with de facto LGBTI grouping and ad-hoc protective isolation.

Human Rights Watch records a Honduran judge describing a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards; the judge informed prosecutors, who did not investigate, and concluded that "there's no way to protect trans women in men's prisons". Her account, given in 2020, is independent confirmation of both the placement rule and official inaction.

Health provision covers all citizens and the government has worked increasingly with non-governmental organisations on HIV/AIDS awareness, but the influence of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant churches has blocked any comprehensive public programme. Female prostitutes and men who have sex with men are identified as the highest-risk groups, and no youth-specific care or medication provisions appear in the sources. The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs also allows "sanitation control" sweeps used to entrap sex workers, a power LGBTQ organisations say police apply against transgender women.

The anti-discrimination articles survived the 2017 Penal Code transition: LGBTQ rights groups met with the National Congress to confirm the wording of Articles 321 and 321-A and both were retained. The new Penal Code took effect in March 2017.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and visa requirements, border screening, and any gender-marker rules on Honduran passports or identity documents are not covered by the source inventory and remain unresolved here. The same applies to whether a visitor's own country documents are inspected against presentation.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights ordered reforms in the 2021 judgment in Vicky Hernández v. Honduras, including legal gender recognition, and Honduras has implemented them only partially. The sources do not specify which elements are complete, which are outstanding, or the domestic mechanism giving the judgment effect; that status is unresolved.

A name change for LGBTI persons is stated to be approved, but no procedure, timeline, documentation requirement or eligibility condition appears in the inventory. Whether legal gender marker change follows from the name change is not sourced.

The Reuters feature referenced for the regional flight pattern returned HTTP 401 and could not be retrieved at research time, so its specific claims are unverified here. The GlobalGayz material is a dated index with embedded excerpts rather than full articles, and functions only as corroborating timeline evidence. No trans-specific incident counts, court outcomes or homicide statistics for the current period appear in the inventory, so the summary's characterisation of risk rests on the 2009, 2017, 2020 and 2021 reporting cited.
